nodes.label: Basic circle terms and radii
nodes.description: Identify and use the basic terms of the circle (centre, radius, chord, diameter, surface of the circle, points inside, on and outside) and use radii and diameters to compare lengths and solve problems.

nodes.label: Axes of symmetry in circle
nodes.description: Describe the axes of symmetry of a circle and state that any straight line through the centre is an axis of symmetry.

nodes.label: Chord–centre perpendicular corollaries
nodes.description: Apply the corollaries relating the centre, a chord and its midpoint or perpendicular to calculate lengths, angles and areas and to prove statements about chords.

nodes.label: Position of a point relative to a circle
nodes.description: Determine the position of a point with respect to a circle by comparing MA with the radius r, and find unknown values (x) from such conditions.

nodes.label: Line and circle; tangents
nodes.description: Determine whether a straight line is outside, a secant or a tangent to a circle by comparing the distance MA with the radius r, and use the perpendicularity of a tangent to the radius at the point of tangency to calculate lengths and angles and to justify that a line is a tangent.

nodes.label: Position of two circles
nodes.description: Determine the position of two circles (distant, touching externally or internally, intersecting, concentric) by comparing MN with r_1 + r_2 and r_1 - r_2.

nodes.label: Line of centers applications
nodes.description: Use the line of centers of touching or intersecting circles, with the common tangent and the common chord, to calculate lengths and angles and to prove relations.

nodes.label: Circle through one point
nodes.description: Draw circles passing through a given point, choosing centers and using the compass, and state that infinitely many such circles exist (equal radii give centers on a congruent circle centered at A).

nodes.label: Circle through two points
nodes.description: Draw circles passing through two given points using the axis of the chord AB for the center, and determine the possible circles for a given radius or diameter, including the smallest radius.

nodes.label: Circle through three points
nodes.description: Draw the circumcircle through three noncollinear points as the intersection of the axes of two sides, identify its center in the triangle, and explain why collinear points give no circle.

nodes.label: Chord length versus distance
nodes.description: Compare the lengths of chords of a circle with their distances from the center, using >, < and =, and find the range of a value from such a comparison.

nodes.label: Equal chords are equidistant
nodes.description: Use the theorem that equal chords are equidistant from the center (also in congruent circles) to find lengths and angles and to prove equalities.

nodes.label: Converse: equidistant chords are equal
nodes.description: Use the converse of the theorem, that chords equidistant from the center(s) are equal in length, to calculate chord lengths and prove chords equal, including in concentric and intersecting circles.

questions.stem: M circle is in each of the following figures and $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ is a tangent: Complete: $m(\angle ADB) = \ldots\ldots\ldots$ (figure: angle 30° at B)
solution: AB is a tangent, so MA ⊥ AB and m(∠MAB) = 90°.
B, M, D are on one line and m(∠B) = 30°, so m(∠AMB) = 90° - 30° = 60°.
MA = MD (radii), so ∠MAD = ∠MDA.
∠AMB is an exterior angle of triangle AMD, so 60° = 2 × m(∠ADB).

questions.stem: M circle is in each of the following figures and $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ is a tangent: Complete: Perimeter $\triangle ABC = \ldots\ldots\ldots$ cm (figure: 60°, AD = 10 cm)
solution: AB is a tangent at D and CD is a diameter, so CD ⊥ AB.
CA = CB (tick marks) and m(∠A) = 60°, so m(∠B) = 60° and the triangle is equilateral.
CD ⊥ AB bisects AB (isosceles triangle), so AB = 2 × AD = 20 cm.
Each side is 20 cm.
Perimeter = 3 × 20 = 60 cm.

questions.stem: M circle is in each of the following figures and $\overleftrightarrow{AB}$ is a tangent: Complete: Perimeter of the figure $ABMD = \ldots\ldots\ldots$ cm (figure: 3 cm, 5 cm, 12 cm)
solution: MA is a radius = 5 cm, and AB is a tangent, so MA ⊥ AB.
MB² = 5² + 12² = 169, so MB = 13 cm.
MD ⊥ AC at D (3 cm), so in right triangle MDA: AD² = 25 - 9 = 16, AD = 4 cm.
Perimeter of ABMD = AB + BM + MD + DA = 12 + 13 + 3 + 4 = 32 cm.

questions.stem: Two circles M and N with radii length of 9 cm and 4 cm respectively. Show the position of each of them with respect to the other in the following cases: A: MN = 13 cm; B: MN = 5 cm; C: MN = 3 cm; D: MN = zero; E: MN = 10 cm; F: MN = 15 cm. MN = 13 cm
solution: $\because MN = 13$ cm $\therefore MN = r_1 + r_2$ $\therefore$ the two circles are touching externally.

questions.stem: Two circles M and N with radii length of 9 cm and 4 cm respectively. Show the position of each of them with respect to the other in the following cases: A: MN = 13 cm; B: MN = 5 cm; C: MN = 3 cm; D: MN = zero; E: MN = 10 cm; F: MN = 15 cm. MN = 5 cm
solution: $\because MN = 5$ cm $\therefore MN = r_1 - r_2$ $\therefore$ the two circles are touching internally.

questions.stem: Two circles M and N with radii length of 9 cm and 4 cm respectively. Show the position of each of them with respect to the other in the following cases: A: MN = 13 cm; B: MN = 5 cm; C: MN = 3 cm; D: MN = zero; E: MN = 10 cm; F: MN = 15 cm. MN = zero

questions.stem: Two circles M and N with radii length of 9 cm and 4 cm respectively. Show the position of each of them with respect to the other in the following cases: A: MN = 13 cm; B: MN = 5 cm; C: MN = 3 cm; D: MN = zero; E: MN = 10 cm; F: MN = 15 cm. MN = 10 cm
solution: $\because MN = 10$ cm $\therefore r_1 - r_2 < MN < r_1 + r_2$ $\therefore$ the two circles are intersecting.

questions.stem: Two circles M and N with radii length of 9 cm and 4 cm respectively. Show the position of each of them with respect to the other in the following cases: A: MN = 13 cm; B: MN = 5 cm; C: MN = 3 cm; D: MN = zero; E: MN = 10 cm; F: MN = 15 cm. MN = 15 cm

questions.stem: In each of the following figures the circles are touching two-by-two. Use the information of each figure and complete: BC = ......... cm
solution: Reading the figure: MN = 5 cm, MC = 3 cm and NC ⊥ MB at C (NC is the radius of N to the tangent point on MB).
In right triangle MCN: NC² = 25 - 9 = 16, so NC = 4 cm = radius of N.
Circles touch internally: MN = r1 - r2, so 5 = r1 - 4 and r1 = 9 cm.
MB = r1 = 9 cm.
BC = MB - MC = 9 - 3 = 6 cm.

questions.stem: In each of the following figures the circles are touching two-by-two. Use the information of each figure and complete: m(∠MDN) = ......... °
solution: Radii read from the figure: M is 3 cm, N is 2 cm, D is 1 cm; circles touch two by two.
Touching externally, distance between centres = sum of radii: MN = 3 + 2 = 5, MD = 3 + 1 = 4, DN = 1 + 2 = 3.
3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5², so m(∠MDN) = 90° (converse of Pythagoras).

questions.stem: In each of the following figures M and N are two intersecting circles at A and B. Complete: AB = .......... cm
solution: The line of centers MN is perpendicular to the common chord AB and bisects it, so AB = 2 × DB and ∠MDB = 90°.
In right triangle MDB: MB = 10 cm and m(∠DMB) = 30°.
The side opposite 30° is half the hypotenuse: DB = 5 cm.

The angle between two lines equals the angle between lines perpendicular to them, so the angle at M equals the 52° between AB and the chord.

questions.stem: Is the center of the circle located on the axis of any chord in it?
solution: The center of the circle is on the axis of the chord AB.
This is true for any chord of the circle.
So the center lies on the axis of any chord in it.

MX = MY, so the chords are equidistant from the center, so AB = CD (converse).

questions.stem: If: $MD=ME$ et $m(\angle B)=65^\circ$. Then: $m(\angle A) = \ldots\ldots\ldots^\circ$

So AB = AC (converse).
In triangle ABC, equal sides give equal angles opposite them, so m(∠C) = m(∠B) = 65°.

questions.stem: $\because \overleftrightarrow{MN}\parallel\overleftrightarrow{BC}$, $\because$ the two circles M and N ........., $A\in\overline{BC}$. $\therefore MX=\ldots$, $\therefore AB = \ldots\ldots\ldots$ $\therefore MX=\ldots$
solution: MN ∥ BC, and MX and NY are both perpendicular to BC.
So the distances from M and N to the line BC are equal.
MX = NY.

questions.stem: $\because \overleftrightarrow{MN}\parallel\overleftrightarrow{BC}$, $\because$ the two circles M and N ........., $A\in\overline{BC}$. $\therefore MX=\ldots$, $\therefore AB = \ldots\ldots\ldots$ $A \in \overline{BC}$
solution: The circles M and N are congruent and MX = NY.
So the chords AB and AC are equidistant from the centers.
By the converse of the theorem, AB = AC.

R.T.P: First: $\overline{ED}\parallel\overline{AB}$; Second: Perimeter $\triangle CDE=\frac{1}{2}$ Perimeter $\triangle ABC$
